title: Group ownership transfer is never executed by any recipe
scenario: Alice creates a group, Bob joins as a plain member. (a) Bob POSTs `/api/state/apps/{a}/workspaces/{w}/groups/{g}/owner/transfer/requests/{rid}` targeting himself and must get 403. (b) Alice transfers ownership to Bob and gets 200; the returned snapshot shows Bob as owner and Alice demoted. (c) Alice replays her original owner-only command (e.g. ban, or a second transfer) with a fresh requestId and must now be denied 403. (d) Alice transfers to a principal who is not a member and must get 404/409.
why_it_matters: owner/transfer is the highest-authority mutation on the group aggregate — it relocates the root of every governance permission (ban, remove, role, admission grant, join-code rotation, topology writes). The OpenAPI entry documents 401/403/404/409 but the corpus never observes a single one of them, so a regression that lets any member seize ownership, or that leaves the old owner still privileged after transfer, would pass every black-box gate.
evidence_of_absence: `grep -rl "owner/transfer" /Users/knuthelge/ProjectLocker/github/ar-eye-hunter/packages/shared-test/black-box-runner/tests/api-v1/` returns nothing. The route is real and registered at apps/api-v1/src/group-state/register-group-membership-routes.ts:185 and specified at apps/api-v1/resources/api-v1-openapi.yaml:1108 with responses 200/401/403/404/409.
corrected:
Gap: group ownership transfer (POST .../groups/{g}/owner/transfer/requests/{rid}) is never exercised over the wire — no recipe sends it, so neither its authorization surface nor its role-swap snapshot is pinned by any black-box assertion.

A recipe (say api-v1-group-ownership-transfer.json) with Alice as founder/owner and Bob joined as a plain active member would assert:

1. plainMemberCannotTransfer — Bob POSTs owner/transfer with newOwnerPrincipalId = Bob. Expect 403 with the api-mutation-failure envelope carrying denial.code 'forbidden-role' and denial.message 'Only active group owners can transfer group ownership.' (group-governance-policy.ts:64-68; 403 from GroupPolicyDeniedError.status). This is the assertion with no coverage anywhere in the repo.

2. ownerTransfersToBob — Alice POSTs the same route with newOwnerPrincipalId = Bob. Expect 200 and, in the returned snapshot, Bob role 'owner' AND Alice role 'admin' (not 'member', not removed) with group.ownerPrincipalId now Bob. The admin demotion is the load-bearing detail (compute-group-membership-mutation.ts:238-241) and is the part a recipe most cheaply protects.

3. replayTransferIsIdempotent — Alice re-sends the identical body on the same requestId path. Expect 200 with the same snapshot revision and requestId echo, matching the corpus-wide strict path-identity rule enforced by packages/tests/shared-test/api-v1-recipe-idempotency-cutover.test.ts (which already lists 'owner/transfer' in its mutationRoutes table at line 82 while no recipe supplies a request for it).

4. demotedOwnerCannotTransferAgain — Alice, now admin, POSTs a second transfer with a fresh requestId. Expect 403 / 'forbidden-role'. NOT a ban: an admin banning a plain member still succeeds, so the claim's "replay her original owner-only command (e.g. ban)" would fail as written. If a governance denial against the new owner is wanted, assert instead that Alice banning Bob returns 403 with 'Group admins can only govern regular members.' (group-governance-policy.ts:70-78).

5. selfTransferIsANoOp — Alice (before step 2) transfers to herself. Expect 200 with an unchanged revision and no 'ownership-transferred' event. This is the only declared-but-unreached allowsNoOp branch for GROUP_OWNERSHIP_TRANSFER in api-v1-state-write-group-causal-evidence.ts:41-44.

6. transferToNonMember — Alice targets a registered principal who never joined. Pin the actual failure, which is GroupMutationRejectedError ('Ownership target must be active.', status 400, code 'group-mutation-rejected'), not the 404/409 the claim assumed. Because api-v1-openapi.yaml:1108 declares only 200/401/403/404/409 for this route, this step doubles as a spec-vs-implementation divergence check.

title: Ban, unban, remove and role-promotion have owner-happy-path coverage only — no denial case
scenario: In one group with owner Alice, member Bob and member Carol: Bob POSTs `.../members/{carol}/ban/requests/{rid}` (expect 403), Bob POSTs `.../members/{carol}/remove/requests/{rid}` (expect 403), Bob PUTs `.../members/{bob}/role/requests/{rid}` with `{"role":"admin"}` self-promoting (expect 403), and Bob POSTs `.../members/{carol}/unban/requests/{rid}` after Alice bans Carol (expect 403). Then Alice promotes Bob to admin (200) and Bob's ban of Carol now succeeds (200) — proving the role grant is what moved the boundary.
why_it_matters: These four routes are the group's entire coercive surface, and each is exercised exactly once, always by the owner, always expecting 200. Nothing in the corpus proves a non-owner is refused. A policy regression that let any member ban, evict or self-promote would be invisible to the black-box gates while every existing recipe stayed green.
evidence_of_absence: Full-corpus scan (script over all 53 recipes, matching method+path against every OpenAPI path template): POST `.../members/{principalId}/ban` n=1 statuses=200 (api-v1-group-ban-governance.json), POST `.../unban` n=1 statuses=200 (same file), POST `.../remove` n=1 statuses=200 (api-v1-group-manager-succession.json), PUT `.../members/{principalId}/role` n=1 statuses=200 (api-v1-rtc-topology-convergence.json:548 `promoteBobThroughPrimary`, alice's header). The four 403s in api-v1-group-ban-governance.json are on the member PUT join/leave route, not on ban/unban.
corrected:
The gap is real; the claim's final proof leg should be tightened. Accurate restatement of what a recipe would assert:

Recipe `api-v1-group-governance-authority` — one group, three authenticated clients: owner Alice (creator), member Bob and member Carol, both joined active via PUT `.../members/{id}/requests/{rid}` with `{"status":"active"}` (200).

Denial phase, all as Bob (Authorization: {bobAuthHeader}, x-client-id: {bobClientId}), each asserting the canonical.v2 envelope `{ "type": "api-mutation-failure", "version": "canonical.v2", "code": "forbidden-role", "status": 403 }`:
1. POST `.../members/{carolClientId}/ban/requests/gov-bob-ban-{runId}` -> 403 forbidden-role.
2. POST `.../members/{carolClientId}/remove/requests/gov-bob-remove-{runId}` -> 403 forbidden-role.
3. PUT `.../members/{bobClientId}/role/requests/gov-bob-selfpromote-{runId}` body `{"role":"admin"}` -> 403 forbidden-role (self-promotion is denied by the same first branch, since Bob is not yet owner/admin).
4. Alice bans Carol: POST `.../members/{carolClientId}/ban/requests/gov-alice-ban-{runId}` -> 200, then GET the group snapshot and assert Carol's member status is `banned`. Bob then POSTs `.../members/{carolClientId}/unban/requests/gov-bob-unban-{runId}` -> 403 forbidden-role.

Grant phase (proves the role, not the identity, moved the boundary):
5. Alice PUTs `.../members/{bobClientId}/role/requests/gov-alice-promote-bob-{runId}` body `{"role":"admin"}` -> 200; assert Bob's role is `admin` in the returned snapshot.
6. Bob (now admin) POSTs `.../members/{carolClientId}/unban/requests/gov-bob-unban-2-{runId}` -> 200, and the snapshot shows Carol no longer `banned`.

Note on the original wording: step 6 should be the *unban*, not a re-ban. Re-banning an already-banned Carol hits the `base.status === status && base.role === role` short-circuit at compute-group-membership-mutation.ts:194 and returns a no-op 200, so the state assertion would be vacuous (the 403-vs-200 flip would still be meaningful, since assertGovernance runs first at line 172, but the observable state change would not be). Unban gives a real status transition to assert.

Optional same-run addition, also uncovered at the HTTP boundary: after step 5, Bob-as-admin POSTs `.../members/{aliceClientId}/ban/requests/gov-admin-bans-owner-{runId}` -> 403 forbidden-role, pinning the second branch of canGovernGroupMember ("Group admins can only govern regular members", group-governance-policy.ts:66-72). That branch is exercised only by a Deno service-level test (apps/api-v1/test/services/group-state-service.test.ts, `admin-ban-admin`), never over HTTP.

title: Director appointment and its contention policy are never exercised
scenario: Group with owner Alice (session active) and members Bob and Carol. (a) Bob POSTs `.../director/appoint/requests/{rid}` while Alice's owner session is active — must be refused, because a plain member may appoint only when no owner/admin session is active. (b) Alice disconnects her session; Bob appoints and gets 200; the snapshot shows only `rallarDirector` changed and Bob's role is unchanged. (c) Carol then appoints while Bob's director session is still active — must be refused. (d) Bob disconnects; Carol appoints and succeeds. (e) A director-appoint body carrying an extra generic metadata key is rejected 400, proving the endpoint cannot be used as a generic metadata write.
why_it_matters: The OpenAPI description (api-v1-openapi.yaml:1141-1160) spells out a four-way liveness-dependent policy — active owners/admins may always appoint; active members may appoint only when no owner/admin session is active and no existing appointment has an active session — plus an explicit non-escalation guarantee ('does not grant owner/admin permissions and does not allow generic group metadata updates'). Every clause of that policy, and the escalation guard, is unverified. The route also carries session-liveness coupling, which is exactly the kind of thing presence churn breaks.
evidence_of_absence: `grep -rl "director/appoint" /Users/.../tests/api-v1/` returns nothing; the route is registered at apps/api-v1/src/group-state/register-group-state-mutation-routes.ts:95 and documented with 200/400/401/403/404/409 at api-v1-openapi.yaml:1141.
corrected:
Gap (restated accurately): the api-v1 black-box corpus never issues POST `.../groups/{groupId}/director/appoint/requests/{requestId}`, so the HTTP contract of director appointment — status mapping, actor binding, and the metadata-patch containment — is unpinned end-to-end. Note the policy semantics themselves are already pinned in-process at apps/api-v1/test/services/group-state-service.test.ts:1440; the recipe's added value is the wire contract.

A recipe would set up owner Alice, members Bob and Carol, each with an active group presence session registered at `.../groups/{groupId}/sessions/{theirAuthSessionId}/requests/...` (the appoint path resolves the target session from `actorSessionId`, so the caller must have a live presence session in that group), and assert:

(a) Bob POSTs director/appoint while Alice's owner presence session is live -> 403, failure body message starting `Forbidden: Only owners/admins can appoint while an owner/admin is online.`, and a follow-up group read showing `group.metadata` still has no `rallarDirector` and `metadataVersion` unchanged. Use the OWNER for this leg, not an admin: the mutation read loads only `ownerPrincipalId` and the incumbent `directorPrincipalId` (resolve-group-mutation-read-identities.ts:23-24), so a non-owner admin is not in the policy snapshot and would not produce this refusal.

(b) POST `.../groups/{groupId}/sessions/{aliceSessionId}/disconnect/requests/...`, then Bob appoints -> 200, and the returned snapshot carries `group.metadata.rallarDirector` = { version: 1, mode: 'appointed-spa', principalId: <Bob's clientId>, sessionId: <Bob's auth sessionId>, epoch: 1, heartbeatTtlMs: <sent value> }, while `members[bob].role` is still `member` and no other metadata key was added or dropped.

(b') Same request repeated with a forged body `actorPrincipalId`/`actorSessionId` naming Carol still appoints BOB — the route overwrites both from the auth session (to-group-state-command.ts:85-86 via `withActor`), so the assertion is that the returned `rallarDirector.principalId` equals the caller, not the body value. This is the one leg no existing test covers at any layer.

(c) Carol appoints while Bob's presence session is still live -> 403 with `Forbidden: Cannot appoint a fallback director while another director is active.` and `rallarDirector.epoch` still 1.

(d) Disconnect Bob's presence session, Carol appoints -> 200 with `rallarDirector.principalId` = Carol and `epoch` = 2 (the epoch increment across a handover is the black-box-visible fact `createRallarGroupDirectorAppointment` produces).

(e) An appoint body carrying `metadata` (or any key outside `requestId`/`actorPrincipalId`/`actorSessionId`/`reason`/`traceId`/`heartbeatTtlMs`) -> 400, proving the endpoint is not a generic metadata write; pair it with `heartbeatTtlMs: 0` -> 400 for the positive-integer rule, and a follow-up read showing metadata untouched.

title: Invite revocation is never called, so revoke-then-accept is unproven
scenario: Alice invites Bob (`POST .../invites/{bob}/requests/{rid}`, 200 — already covered). Then: (a) Carol, a non-manager, POSTs `.../invites/{bob}/revoke/requests/{rid}` and gets 403. (b) Alice revokes and gets 200. (c) Bob POSTs `.../invites/accept/requests/{rid}` and is refused — the revoked invite must not be redeemable. (d) Alice revokes an invite that was already accepted, or one that never existed, and gets 404. (e) Optionally: revoke and accept issued against the same invite across two nodes, asserting exactly one of the two wins.
why_it_matters: Invite issue and invite accept are both covered (n=12 and n=6, both 200-only), so the corpus proves a credential can be minted and redeemed but never that it can be withdrawn. Revocation is the only mechanism to un-invite someone from an invite-only group; if revoke silently no-ops, or if an in-flight accept beats a revoke, an evicted principal retains a standing path back into the group and nothing detects it.
evidence_of_absence: `grep -rl "/revoke/" /Users/.../tests/api-v1/` returns nothing. The route is registered at apps/api-v1/src/group-state/register-group-admission-routes.ts:260 (operation `revoke-group-invite`, dispatched in apps/api-v1/src/group-state/to-group-state-command.ts:379) and documented at api-v1-openapi.yaml:869 with 200/401/403/404.
corrected:
Gap (restated accurately): the invite revoke route `POST .../groups/{groupId}/invites/{principalId}/revoke/requests/{requestId}` is never exercised by any black-box recipe, so revocation's real semantics are unproven end-to-end. A new recipe (e.g. `api-v1-group-invite-revocation.json`) should create the group with `"joinMode": "invite-only"` — not the corpus-default `"open"` — because only invite-only makes redemption refusable, and assert:

1. Alice (owner) invites Bob: 200, snapshot member `{principalId: bob, status: "invited"}` (this half is already covered in api-v1-group-admission-approval.json step `ownerInvitesThePendingPrincipal`).
2. Carol (authenticated, not a member / not a lifecycle manager) POSTs the revoke: 403 with body `{"type":"api-mutation-failure","version":"canonical.v2","status":403}` and the governance denial code from `canGovernGroupMember` — the recipe pins the code the real server emits.
3. Alice revokes: 200, and the snapshot shows Bob as `status: "left"` (computeRevokeInvite transitions the invited row via `transitionGroupMemberLifecycle(..., 'left', audit)` and emits `eventType: 'member-left'`). Optionally assert the `member-left` event on a WS group-state subscription, since `state-write-group-event-semantics-evidence.test.ts` pins that event name but no recipe observes it.
4. Bob POSTs `.../invites/accept/requests/{rid}`: 403 with `code: "group-invite-required"` and message "A valid invite is required to join." — this is the load-bearing assertion, that a revoked invite is not redeemable, and it is only expressible under invite-only.
5. Idempotency / no-op, NOT 404: Alice revokes a second time, and Alice revokes a principal who was never invited — both return **200 with the snapshot unchanged** (`existing?.status !== 'invited'` -> `noOp`, outcome `no-op`). Same for revoking an already-accepted (`status: "active"`) invite. This pins the documented-404 vs actual-200-no-op divergence in api-v1-openapi.yaml, where the route's 404 only fires for group-not-found.
6. Optional race tier (genuinely new — `api-v1-state-write-convergence.json` races only member-activate, session connect/reconnect and topology/config, never `/invites/`): a `parallel` step issuing Alice's revoke on the primary node and Bob's accept on the secondary node against the same invite, asserting exactly one succeeds and the converged snapshot reads either `left` (revoke won) or `active` (accept won) on both nodes — never a split.

title: The whole admin surface is never hit by an authenticated non-admin principal
scenario: A single recipe: log in as `alice` (a normal principal, not in AUTH_ADMIN_CLIENT_IDS) and, with her valid bearer token and x-client-id, call each admin family once — `GET /api/admin/operations/overview`, `GET /api/admin/operations/state`, `POST /api/admin/operations/maintenance/prune-expired/requests/{rid}`, `POST /api/admin/operations/crdt/erase/requests/{rid}`, `POST /api/admin/support/explain/group`, `POST /api/crdt/admin/documents/list` — asserting a denial (403/401) and, critically, an error body that carries no diagnostic payload. Then repeat the same calls as `admin` to prove the same requests succeed, so the recipe pins the boundary rather than a blanket refusal.
why_it_matters: Every admin negative case in the corpus is 'no bearer token at all'. The gate that actually matters is membership in `adminClientIds` (apps/api-v1/src/crdt/register-crdt-admin-routes.ts:295-297, apps/api-v1/src/crdt/create-api-crdt-inbox-service.ts:131) — the difference between an unauthenticated stranger and a logged-in ordinary user. These routes return operational internals, export CRDT debug bundles, prune persisted state and erase documents. A regression that widened the admin predicate would be caught by no recipe.
evidence_of_absence: Every `"403"` occurrence under an /api/admin or /api/crdt path in the corpus is inside an openapi.json body assertion, not a request: api-v1-admin-operations.json:345,360 and api-v1-admin-support.json:177,192 sit inside the `openApiListsAdminOperations` / `openApiListsAdminSupport` steps. A step-by-step dump of api-v1-admin-operations.json and api-v1-admin-support.json shows every admin call is either unauthenticated (401) or made as clientId `admin`; api-v1-idempotency-contract.json uses `{adminAuthHeader}` for its CRDT compact and admin-operation steps.
corrected:
Restate the gap as an authenticated-non-admin denial sweep whose centre of gravity is the CRDT admin read guard, not the admin surface generally.

A recipe (`api-v1-admin-authorization-boundary`) that: registers and logs in `alice` with generated credentials (as `api-v1-spa-statistics.json` already does at `registerAlice` / `loginAlice`), then issues one request per admin family with `Authorization: {aliceAuthHeader}` and `x-client-id: {aliceClientId}`, asserting each is refused by the real config-derived `AUTH_ADMIN_CLIENT_IDS` allow-list:

- `GET /api/admin/operations/overview` and `GET /api/admin/operations/state` -> `status 403`, body exactly `{"error": "Forbidden: platform admin authorization required"}`
- `POST /api/admin/support/explain/group` -> `status 403`, same body

title: Cross-principal client-state reads never test the denial, and the client list route is never called at all
scenario: Alice and Bob both log in and both have client state. Then Bob calls, with his own token: `GET .../clients/{aliceId}`, `GET .../clients/{aliceId}/presence`, `GET .../clients/{aliceId}/events`, `GET .../clients/{aliceId}/events/page` — each must be 403 with no snapshot leaked. Both are privacy boundaries over presence, event history and device instances. Neither is verified. The recipe named `api-v1-cross-principal-client-state-isolation.json` is misleading here — it proves WS event isolation and issues no cross-principal HTTP read.

Gap A — the HTTP strict-read denial is never exercised. Note the corpus already covers cross-principal isolation on the *WebSocket* side in this same recipe; what is missing is the REST denial. Add four steps, each a `GET` sent with `{bobAuthHeader}` plus `x-client-id: {bobClientId}` against Alice's principal:
  - `GET /api/state/apps/{applicationId}/workspaces/{workspaceId}/clients/{aliceClientId}`
  - `.../clients/{aliceClientId}/presence`
  - `.../clients/{aliceClientId}/events`
  - `.../clients/{aliceClientId}/events/page`
Each asserts `status: 403` with body exactly `{"error": "Forbidden: state read principal id does not match authenticated client"}` — verified to carry no `code` key, because `toClientStateRouteErrorResponse` only emits `code` when the message itself parses as JSON, which this plain string does not. The assertion that matters is the negative one: the response body must contain no `principalId`, `stateRevision`, `presence`, or `events` field, i.e. no snapshot leak. This pins the two *separate* code paths that produce the same status by different means — `assertSelfWhenStrict` in `client-state-point-read-route.ts` (plain `Error`, status inferred from the `Forbidden:` prefix) for the point read, and `assertCanReadClientState` in `client-state-routes.ts` (typed `RequestAuthFailure` carrying `status: 403`) for the other three. Of these four, the existing Deno route test covers only the point read and `/events/page` with stubs; `/presence` and `/events` have no test anywhere.

Gap B — the list route `GET /api/state/apps/{applicationId}/workspaces/{workspaceId}/clients` (`api-v1-openapi.yaml:304`) has literally zero recipe coverage. Add one step calling it as Bob (`{bobAuthHeader}` + `x-client-id: {bobClientId}`) asserting `200` and an array of exactly one element whose `principalId` equals `{bobClientId}` — with Alice's client state provably present in the same scope, since the recipe already created it. title: WebSocket upgrade has no negative-path recipe: no reused, expired, foreign or missing ticket
scenario: Alice issues a WS ticket. (a) Open `/api/ws/{aliceSession}?ticket={t}` successfully, then attempt a second socket with the same ticket `t` — must be refused (single-use). (b) Attempt `/api/ws/{aliceSession}` with no `ticket` query parameter — 401. (c) Issue Bob a ticket and attempt `/api/ws/{aliceSession}?ticket={bobTicket}` — the session/ticket mismatch must be refused, proving a ticket cannot be redeemed against another principal's session. (d) Plain `GET /api/ws/{aliceSession}?ticket={t}` with no `Upgrade: websocket` header — 426.
why_it_matters: The WS ticket is the sole credential on the realtime plane and the spec calls it 'short-lived one-time' (api-v1-openapi.yaml:280-303). Twenty-two recipes open sockets and every single one uses a fresh, valid, correctly-paired ticket. Ticket single-use is proven only for the *different* agent-session-ticket route (`/api/auth/agent-session-tickets/consume`, 404 on reuse). If `/api/ws` stopped consuming tickets, or stopped binding a ticket to its session id, every recipe would still pass — and a leaked ticket would become a reusable, transferable realtime credential.
evidence_of_absence: `grep -rniE "invalid.?ticket|expired.?ticket|reused?.?ticket|bogus|tampered|forged"` over all 53 recipes returns nothing; `grep -rn "426\|Upgrade: websocket"` returns nothing. All 22 files containing `/api/ws/` use it inside `set` steps concatenating a freshly-issued `?ticket=` value. The handler's 426 and 401 branches are at apps/api-v1/src/routes/ws-routes.ts:45-56.
corrected:
Restated gap: no recipe asserts the 401 refusal side of GET /api/ws/{sessionId}. A new recipe (say api-v1-websocket-upgrade-auth) would, using the existing `api` http connection and a request header "Upgrade": "websocket" so the 426 gate at ws-routes.ts:46 is passed:

1. missingTicketRefused — GET /api/ws/{alphaSessionId} with the Upgrade header and NO ticket query parameter; expect status 401 and body {"error":"Unauthorized: Missing websocket auth ticket"}. This branch (request-auth-service.ts:102) has no coverage anywhere in the repo.
2. redeemedTicketRefused — issue alphaWsTicket, open the real socket with ws.open (which consumes it), then GET /api/ws/{alphaSessionId}?ticket={alphaWsTicket} with the Upgrade header; expect 401 {"error":"Unauthorized: Invalid or expired websocket auth ticket"}, and expect the already-open wsAlpha connection to receive no close (ws.wait absence), proving redemption is single-use against the real AppInbox ticket row rather than a stubbed Map.
3. foreignSessionTicketRefused — register/login a second principal beta, issue betaWsTicket for {betaSessionId}, then GET /api/ws/{alphaSessionId}?ticket={betaWsTicket} with the Upgrade header; expect 401, proving the expectedSessionId binding at request-auth-service.ts:108 is enforced end to end, then confirm betaWsTicket is still redeemable by opening ws on /api/ws/{betaSessionId}?ticket={betaWsTicket} (i.e. the failed cross-session attempt must not have burned Beta's ticket).

Drop the 426 limb — apps/api-v1/test/composition/create-api-v1-route-installers.test.ts:29 already asserts it against the real assembled app. Drop "expired" — the TTL is server configuration (dependencies.authentication.webSocketTicketTtlMs, register-auth-credential-mutation-routes.ts:112), not a per-request field, so a recipe cannot age a ticket out without changing the whole run's server config.
proof:
ABSENCE IN CORPUS (verified, both empty):
  $ grep -rn '"path": *"/api/ws' packages/shared-test/black-box-runner/tests/api-v1/*.json  -> exit=1 (no output)
  $ grep -rniE '"upgrade"|Unauthorized: (Missing websocket|Invalid or expired websocket)' packages/shared-test/black-box-runner/tests/ -> exit2=1 (no output)
Every /api/ws/ hit in tests/api-v1 is a `set` step, e.g. api-v1-group-state-reconnect-resync.json "deriveAlphaWsUrlSecond": {"type":"set","transform":{"concat":[{"path":"variables.rallarWsBaseUrl"},"/api/ws/",{"path":"outputs.alphaSessionId"},"?ticket=",{"urlEncode":{"path":"outputs.alphaWsTicketSecond"}}]}} — and that recipe issues a SECOND fresh ticket ("createAlphaWsTicketSecond") for the reconnect rather than reusing the first, so single-use is respected but never asserted. api-v1-auth-session.json's only ws-ticket negative is "rejectWebSocketTicketWithoutAuth" -> POST /api/auth/ws-ticket/... expect 401, i.e. the ISSUE endpoint, not the upgrade route; its parallel race is over /api/auth/agent-session-tickets/consume, a different ticket type.

THE BRANCHES EXIST ON THE REAL SERVER:

  packages/shared-server/http/request-auth-service.ts:102  throw unauthorized('Missing websocket auth ticket');
  :108  expectedSessionId: input.sessionId

  apps/api-v1/test/composition/create-api-v1-route-installers.test.ts:29

title: Group listing is only ever called unauthenticated — its scoping is never verified
scenario: Alice creates a group in application A / workspace W; Bob creates one in application B / workspace W. Bob then calls `GET /api/state/apps/{A}/workspaces/{W}/groups` with his own valid session and the result must not contain Alice's group. Alice calls the same path and sees hers. Additionally, with a group whose visibility parks a pending principal (the admission-approval flow already builds one), a pending principal's listing must not expose the group body it is forbidden to read point-wise.
why_it_matters: `GET .../groups` is the only bulk-read of the group aggregate, and the corpus calls it exactly twice — both times without credentials, asserting 401. It is never called successfully. api-v1-scope-isolation.json proves cross-scope denial for the *point* read (`GET .../groups/{groupId}` → 403) but never for the list, so a list handler that ignores scope, or that returns bodies the point read would refuse, is a straight enumeration leak that no recipe would catch.
evidence_of_absence: Route-coverage scan: `GET .../workspaces/{workspaceId}/groups` n=2, statuses={401} only, both in api-v1-auth-session.json:327 (`rejectMissingBearerToken`) and :342 (`rejectMissingClientIdHeader`). The 403 point-read pair `rejectBobReadScopeAGroup` / `rejectAliceReadScopeBGroup` in api-v1-scope-isolation.json target `.../groups/{sharedGroupId}`, not the collection.
corrected:
Restate the gap as: "The authenticated group-collection read is never exercised — neither its scope filter nor its active-membership filter is observed."

A recipe would assert, using two runId-unique scopes as api-v1-scope-isolation.json already builds (both defining the same `{sharedGroupId}`):

1. `listScopeAGroupsAsAlice` — GET `/api/state/apps/{scopeAApplicationId}/workspaces/{scopeAWorkspaceId}/groups` with `{aliceAuthHeader}` + `x-client-id: {aliceClientId}` -> 200, body compared under `"comparison": "compatible-complete"` against a single-element array `[{ group: { groupId: "{sharedGroupId}" }, members: [{ principalId: "{aliceClientId}", status: "active" }] }]`. `compatible-complete` is what makes this non-vacuous: it fails if scope B's identically-named group leaks in.
2. `rejectBobListScopeAGroups` — the same GET with `{bobAuthHeader}` -> 200 with body `[]` under `compatible-complete`. This is the load-bearing assertion: it pins both filters at once (Bob is authenticated, in scope, and still sees nothing because he is not an active member), and it is the collection-level analogue of the existing point-read pair `rejectBobReadScopeAGroup` / `rejectAliceReadScopeBGroup`.
3. The mirrored pair in scope B (`listScopeBGroupsAsBob` -> exactly Bob's group; `rejectAliceListScopeBGroups` -> `[]`), which is what actually proves cross-application/workspace scoping rather than mere membership filtering, since the two groups share one groupId.

Plus, inside api-v1-group-admission-approval.json, immediately after `pendingReadVisibilityIsLimited` (403) and again after `managerGrantsToActive`:

4. `pendingPrincipalListingOmitsGroup` — GET the collection with `{bobAuthHeader}` -> 200 whose body under `compatible-complete` does not include `{approvalGroupId}` (status `pending` maps to visibility `invite`, not `full`), proving the collection cannot hand out the body the point read just refused.
5. `grantedPrincipalListingIncludesGroup` — the same GET after the grant -> 200 including `{approvalGroupId}` with `members[].status: "active"`, proving the filter tracks membership transitions and the assertion in (4) was not vacuously passing on an always-empty list.

An optional sixth step in api-v1-group-ban-governance (GET the collection as the banned principal -> group absent) extends the same filter to the `'none'` visibility branch.
proof:
ABSENCE (exact grep, whole runner tree):

  $ grep -rn '"path": "/api/state/apps/{applicationId}/workspaces/{workspaceId}/groups"' packages/shared-test/black-box-runner/tests/
  packages/shared-test/black-box-runner/tests/api-v1/api-v1-auth-session.json:332
  packages/shared-test/black-box-runner/tests/api-v1/api-v1-auth-session.json:347

Widened to any collection form incl. query string, across all of packages/shared-test:

  $ grep -rnE '"path": "[^"]*/groups(\?[^"]*)?"' packages/shared-test/
  .../docs/black-box-runner-recipe-guide.md:267         (doc sample)
  .../examples/rallar-server-negative-auth.json:33,48   (example, not registered)
  .../tests/api-v1/api-v1-auth-session.json:332,347

Both recipe hits are 401 negatives: `"name": "rejectMissingBearerToken"` (no headers, `"status": 401, "error": "Unauthorized: Missing bearer token"`) and `"name": "rejectMissingClientIdHeader"` (`"status": 401, "error": "Unauthorized: Missing x-client-id header"`). No recipe anywhere sends this GET with `{aliceAuthHeader}`/`{bobAuthHeader}`.

THE BEHAVIOUR THAT GOES UNOBSERVED — apps/api-v1/src/group-state/register-group-state-read-routes.ts:22,30,47-52:

  const GROUPS_PATH = '/api/state/apps/:applicationId/workspaces/:workspaceId/groups';
  app.get(GROUPS_PATH, (context) => readGroupSnapshotList(context, dependencies, authorization));
  ...
  const snapshots = authSession
      ? (await dependencies.groupStateService.listSnapshots(toGroupStateRouteScope(context)))
          .filter((snapshot) => isGroupStateRouteSnapshotReadable(snapshot, authSession.clientId))
      : await dependencies.groupStateService.listSnapshots(toGroupStateRouteScope(context));

`isGroupStateRouteSnapshotReadable` -> `canReadGroupSnapshot`, and packages/shared-server/rallar-system/group-state/policy/group-snapshot-visibility-policy.ts returns allowed only for `visibility === 'full'`; `readGroupVisibility` maps member status `'pending'` and non-expired `'invited'` to `'invite'`, `'removed'`/`'banned'` to `'none'`. Strict mode is live in black-box runs — apps/api-v1/resources/.env:2 `RALLAR_STATE_STRICT_READ_AUTH='1'` (and packages/tests/repo/api-v1-black-box-workflow.test.ts:40 lists it among required env). WHY EXISTING UNIT COVERAGE DOES NOT CLOSE IT — apps/api-v1/test/group-state/group-state-read-routes.test.ts:74-101, `Deno.test('canonical group list reads filter snapshots with strict-read authorization')`:

  const allowedSnapshot = createGroupStateRouteSnapshot('room-1', ['alice']);
  const deniedSnapshot  = createGroupStateRouteSnapshot('room-2', ['bob']);
  listSnapshots: () => Promise.resolve([allowedSnapshot, deniedSnapshot]),
  requireApiAuthSession: () => Promise.resolve(createGroupStateRouteAuthSession('alice')),

The service is stubbed, so the scope argument is never honoured by anything real: a `listSnapshots` that ignored applicationId/workspaceId would still pass. And the repository-level tests never build a second scope:

  $ grep -n "app-2\|workspace-2\|other-app\|application-b" packages/tests/api-v1/client-and-group-state-repositories.test.ts
  (no output)

Every `listSnapshots(...)` call in that file uses `applicationId: 'app-1', workspaceId: 'workspace-1'`. Nothing in packages/tests/ or apps/api-v1/test/ asserts that the collection excludes another application's or workspace's groups.

EXPRESSIBLE TODAY: prerequisite state already exists — api-v1-scope-isolation.json:6-26 defines runId-unique `scopeAApplicationId`/`scopeBApplicationId` and one `sharedGroupId` used in both scopes (so a list body is deterministic), and api-v1-group-admission-approval.json:238 `uninvitedJoinParksPending` (`"status": "pending"`) followed by :264 `pendingReadVisibilityIsLimited` (`"status": 403`) parks the pending principal one GET away from the collection. The non-vacuous array assertion is already supported and used: `"comparison": "compatible-complete"` at api-v1-state-write-convergence.json:353,549,743 and api-v1-read-your-writes-presence.json:204, documented as "keeps extra object keys tolerated but rejects unexpected array elements".

title: Six admin-operations read/reset routes are never called
scenario: As `admin`, after a formation burst has produced real state: `GET /api/admin/operations/state` and `GET /api/admin/operations/state/apps/{a}/workspaces/{w}` (asserting the scoped view is a strict subset of the global one), `GET /api/admin/operations/crdt` and `GET /api/admin/operations/crdt/apps/{a}/workspaces/{w}`, `GET /api/admin/operations/system`, then `POST /api/admin/operations/metrics/reset` followed by a re-read of `GET /api/admin/operations/overview` proving the counters actually moved to zero.
why_it_matters: `metrics/reset` is a mutation on the operator's observability plane, and the scoped variants (`/state/apps/{a}/workspaces/{w}`, `/crdt/apps/{a}/workspaces/{w}`) are cross-tenant read boundaries — the scoped path must not return another application's operational state. Only three of the twelve admin-operations read routes (`overview`, `queues`, `realtime`) are ever called. This matters more than usual because the formation-burst recipes already assert on `/queues` and `/realtime`, so operator metrics are load-bearing for existing gates while most of the surface producing them is unverified.
evidence_of_absence: `grep -rhn '"path": "/api/admin/operations/[a-z/-]*' /Users/.../tests/api-v1/ | sort -u` yields only `overview`, `queues`, `realtime`, `maintenance/prune-expired`, `topology/recompute`, `crdt/lifecycle`, `crdt/erase`. Route-coverage scan marks `/state`, `/state/apps/{a}/workspaces/{w}`, `/crdt`, `/crdt/apps/{a}/workspaces/{w}`, `/system`, `/metrics/reset`, `/crdt/integrity`, `/crdt/debug-export` and `/crdt/compact/requests/{rid}` as zero-coverage (api-v1-openapi.yaml:2417-2677).
corrected:
Restated gap (two uncovered behaviours, not six uncalled routes):

(1) Application/workspace-scoped admin aggregation is never executed. A recipe should, after a formation burst has created groups/members/sessions in workspace A and at least one group plus one CRDT document in workspace B, call as `admin`:
  - `GET /api/admin/operations/state` (global) and `GET /api/admin/operations/state/apps/{A}/workspaces/{wA}`, asserting the scoped response echoes `scope: {applicationId, workspaceId}` (the global one omits it), that `groups.activeGroups`, `groups.totalActiveMembers`, `clients.activeSessions` and `events.recentGroupEvents` are each ≤ the global figure, and — the real leak test — that the workspace-B scoped read reports counts that exclude the workspace-A groups (i.e. scopedA.activeGroups + scopedB.activeGroups ≤ global.activeGroups, and scopedB does not include A's member count).
  - `GET /api/admin/operations/crdt` and `GET /api/admin/operations/crdt/apps/{A}/workspaces/{wA}`, asserting `documents.total` and `storage.updates`/`storage.snapshots` are scoped-down, and that a document created in workspace B is absent from the workspace-A scoped `byScopeType`/`byLifecycle` breakdown.
This is the only way to execute `PSqlAdminStateReader.readScoped` and the scoped branches of `PSqlAdminCrdtReader`; `/overview` reaches only `readGlobal`.

(2) `POST /api/admin/operations/metrics/reset` is never called. A recipe should, on the same connection that served the formation burst, first `GET /api/admin/operations/realtime` (or `/overview`) and capture non-zero `groupFormation.metrics`/`rtcTopology.metrics`, then `POST /api/admin/operations/metrics/reset` with `{ "categories": ["group-formation"], "reason": "..." }` asserting `operation: "metrics.reset"`, `status: "completed"`, `changed: true`, and that the response's own `before.groupFormation` counters are non-zero while `after.groupFormation` counters are zero; then a bodyless `POST` (no `categories`) asserting the default-all-categories path also returns `changed: true` and zeroed `after.rtcTopology`. Follow with a same-connection `GET /api/admin/operations/overview` asserting `realtime.groupFormationMetrics` is at or below the reset `after` values — assert "not greater than", not strict zero, because formation metrics can tick again from post-reset reconcile activity, and because `read-admin-realtime.ts` flags these metrics `process-local-realtime` (in the cluster profile a reset on one server does not clear another's).

Not part of the gap: direct calls to the global `GET /api/admin/operations/state`, `/crdt` and `/system` add only response-shape breadth — those readers already run on every existing `/overview` step in api-v1-admin-operations.json.
proof:
Absence in the corpus — every `operations/...` path literal in the whole recipe tree:

$ grep -rho 'operations/[a-zA-Z0-9/{}._-]*' packages/shared-test/black-box-runner/tests/
  operations/crdt/erase/requests/…
  operations/crdt/lifecycle/requests/…
  operations/maintenance/prune-expired/requests/…
  operations/overview
  operations/queues
  operations/realtime
  operations/topology/recompute/requests/…

No `operations/state`, `operations/state/apps/...`, bare `operations/crdt`, `operations/crdt/apps/...`, `operations/system`, or `operations/metrics/reset`.

    const [queues, state, crdt, system, realtime] = await Promise.all([
        this.options.readQueues(input), this.options.readState(input),

Why the SCOPED variants are NOT covered — register-admin-operation-read-routes.ts:57-64 calls `dependencies.operations.overview.execute({ adminSession })` with no `scope`, and packages/shared-server/rallar-system/admin-operations/postgres/p-sql-admin-state-reader.ts:59 branches on it:
    return input.scope ? await this.readScoped(input.scope) : await this.readGlobal();
`readScoped` (lines 62-82) issues entirely different queries (scoped `readLiveRuntimeRows`, `clientState.readScopedFacts`, `countRecentGroupEvents(scope)`); p-sql-admin-crdt-reader.ts:63-107 likewise switches to `where application_id = ${scope.applicationId} and workspace_id = ${scope.workspaceId}`. title: Three of five admin-support explain routes exist only as an OpenAPI assertion
scenario: As `admin`, after a formation recipe has produced a real group and a real client: `POST /api/admin/support/explain/client` with Alice's principal (200, narrative naming her sessions), `POST /api/admin/support/explain/group` with a scoped `GroupRef` — plus the same call with a bare group id, since the spec explicitly prefers the scoped form — and `POST /api/admin/support/explain/crdt-document` against a document the CRDT recipes already seed, asserting the debug bundle in the narrative is redacted by default. Each also called as a non-admin authenticated principal, expecting 403, and against a non-existent target, expecting 404.
why_it_matters: These routes render diagnostic narratives over another principal's client state, a group's internals, and CRDT document contents — they are read amplification for support staff and the highest-value target for a privilege check. The two that are covered (`explain/request`, `explain/queue-item`) are both called against deliberately *missing* targets, so no explain route in the corpus has ever rendered a narrative over real data. The redaction-by-default promise on `explain/crdt-document` is asserted nowhere.
evidence_of_absence: `grep -rhn '"path": "/api/admin/support/explain/[a-z-]*"' /Users/.../tests/api-v1/` yields only `queue-item` and `request`. `explain/client` appears once in the corpus, at api-v1-admin-support.json:166, inside the `openApiListsAdminSupport` body assertion; `explain/group` and `explain/crdt-document` do not appear at all (`grep -rl "explain/group"` and `grep -rl "explain/crdt-document"` both return nothing). The step-by-step dump of api-v1-admin-support.json confirms its only two real calls are `explainMissingQueueItem` and `explainRequestWithoutIndexedTarget`.
corrected:
Gap: `POST /api/admin/support/explain/client`, `.../explain/group` and `.../explain/crdt-document` are never called by any black-box recipe, so nothing proves the api-v1 composition root wires the real state services into admin support, nor that the three narratives are populated from state a real flow produced.

A recipe (extending `api-v1-admin-support.json`, reusing its `loginDemoAdmin` + `deriveAdminAuthHeader` steps) would assert:

1. explain/client, populated. Run a formation/join flow so Alice has a real client snapshot and an open WS connection, then POST `{ scope: { applicationId, workspaceId }, principalId: <alice>, sessionId: <her session>, limitRecentEvents: 5 }`. Expect 200 with `target.kind === 'client'`, `rawRefs[0]` equal to `client:<applicationId>/<workspaceId>/<alice>`, and — the load-bearing part — facts that came from a live `clientStateService` and `wsStatus`, i.e. NOT the `hasClientStateService: false` degraded shape from `clientWarnings`, and a non-empty `timeline` built from her real client events.

2. explain/client, unknown principal. Same scope, a principal that never existed. Expect 200 (not 404), with the absence carried as facts/warnings. This pins the divergence from the spec, which declares a `404` response that no code path can produce.

3. explain/group, scoped ref. POST `{ groupRef: { applicationId, workspaceId, groupId }, limitRecentEvents: 20 }` for the group the formation steps created. Expect 200, `target.kind === 'group'`, a real `snapshot`-derived fact set plus a `topologyView` and a lifecycle-policy fact — proving `topologyQuery` and `readLifecyclePolicy` are actually supplied, rather than the `hasTopologyQuery: false` / `hasLifecyclePolicyReader: false` warning shape.

4. explain/group, malformed shape. POST `{ groupId: "room-1" }` (a bare id, the form the spec's prose warns against). Expect 400 with an "unexpected field groupId" style error — the decoder's `requireExactKeys` contract, currently pinned only by a Deno unit test.

5. explain/crdt-document, default. Seed a document the way `api-v1-crdt-append-history.json` does (`documentType: "black-box-map"`, `documentId: "crdt-history-...-{runId}"`), then POST `{ document: {...} }` with no flags. Expect 200 with `crdt.metadata` fact `value: 'found'`, `certainty: 'exact'`, `rawRefs[0]` of the form `crdt:<documentKey>`, and NO debug bundle and NO integrity report in the response.

6. explain/crdt-document, bundle requested. Same document with `{ includeIntegrity: true, includeRedactedDebugBundle: true }`. Expect 200 where the returned bundle carries the server-forced redaction marker (`payloadsRedacted: true`, reason `api-v1-admin-support-redaction`) and no document payload bodies — proving redaction is not caller-controllable over the wire.

Drop from the original scenario: the 404-on-missing-target expectations (unreachable), the "bare group id as an alternate accepted form" framing (it is a 400), and "redacted by default" (by default there is no bundle at all). The 401/403 admin gate is shared by all five routes through one `requireAdminSession` and is already covered at line 27 of the recipe, so re-asserting it per route adds nothing.
proof:
Absence, corpus-wide (`packages/shared-test`, `packages/tests`, `apps/rallar-black-box`, non-.ts files): the only hit for any of the three routes is `packages/shared-test/black-box-runner/tests/api-v1/api-v1-admin-support.json:166: "/api/admin/support/explain/client": {` — which is inside the `openApiListsAdminSupport` `expect.body.paths` assertion (step at line 155), not a request. `grep -rl "explain/group"` and `grep -rl "explain/crdt-document"` over `tests/api-v1/` both return nothing. The only real request paths in the corpus are `"path": "/api/admin/support/explain/queue-item"` (lines 32, 99) and `"path": "/api/admin/support/explain/request"` (line 135).

Routes exist and are wired: `apps/api-v1/src/routes/admin-support-routes.ts` registers all five, e.g. `app.post('/api/admin/support/explain/group', (context) => respondToAdminSupportRequest(context, dependencies, { decode: decodeAdminSupportExplainGroupRequest, write: (input) => dependencies.support.explainGroup(input) }))`, installed at `apps/api-v1/src/composition/create-api-v1-route-installers.ts:297`. Real dependencies are wired at `create-api-v1-admin-services.ts:60-71` and `create-default-rallar-server.ts:144: crdtAdminRepository: crdtLogRepository`.

Correction 1 — no bare-group-id form exists. `apps/api-v1/src/routes/admin-support-request-decoding.ts` does `requireExactKeys(request, ['groupRef', 'principalId', 'sessionId', 'limitRecentEvents'], 'Admin support group request')` and `requireExactKeys(groupRef, ['applicationId', 'workspaceId', 'groupId'], 'Admin support groupRef')`. A bare `groupId` is a 400 "unexpected field", proven by `apps/api-v1/test/routes/admin-support-request-decoding.test.ts` asserting `/unexpected field unsupportedField/`. The OpenAPI "Prefer scoped `GroupRef` input over bare group ids" is prose, not a second accepted shape.

Correction 2 — no 404 is reachable on these three routes. `grep -rn "not found\|notFound" packages/shared-server/rallar-system/admin-support/` returns exactly one hit, `statistics/group-statistics-service.ts:35` (a different route). `client-admin-support.ts`, `group-admin-support.ts` and `crdt-admin-support.ts` never throw for a missing target; they pass `snapshot`/`metadata` as `undefined` into the projections, which emit e.g. `{ label: 'crdt.metadata', source: 'crdt-admin-log', value: 'missing', certainty: 'unavailable' }` and return 200. The `'404': $ref: '#/components/responses/NotFound'` at `api-v1-openapi.yaml` for `explain/client`, `explain/group` and `explain/crdt-document` is an unreachable declaration — itself worth pinning.

Correction 3 — the debug bundle is absent by default, not "redacted by default". `crdt-admin-support.ts`: `const debugBundle = input.request.includeRedactedDebugBundle === true ? await repository?.exportDebugBundle?.(input.request.document, { reason: 'api-v1-admin-support-debug-export', exportedAtEpochMs: this.dependencies.now(), redaction: { payloadsRedacted: true, reason: 'api-v1-admin-support-redaction' } }) : undefined;`. title: Graph diagnostic reads are documented in a recipe but never requested
scenario: After a managed formation burst has published a layout: `GET .../workspaces/{w}/graphs/global` as an authenticated principal (200) and with no bearer token (401, exercising the `strictReadAuthorization` branch); `GET .../groups/{g}/graphs/latest` as a member (200, edges consistent with the same group's `GET .../topology`), as a non-member in another scope (403), and against an unknown group id (404).

evidence_of_absence: Route-coverage scan: `GET .../graphs/global` and `GET .../groups/{groupId}/graphs/latest` both zero-coverage. Their only appearance in the corpus is inside the `openApiListsGraphTopologyAuth` body assertion at api-v1-openapi-topology-auth.json:37 and :51, which is a `GET /api/openapi.json` step. Handlers registered at apps/api-v1/src/routes/graph-topology-routes.ts:121 and :136.

Gap (restated): the graph diagnostic reads `GET .../workspaces/{w}/graphs/global` and `GET .../groups/{g}/graphs/latest` are documented in the OpenAPI contract the corpus asserts, but no recipe ever issues them. A new recipe (e.g. api-v1-graph-diagnostics-read.json), run after a managed formation burst on one node (reuse the setup shape of api-v1-group-formation-managed-burst-medium.json), would assert:

1. `GET .../graphs/global` with no Authorization header -> 401. This is the only place `assertCanReadScopedGlobalGraph` is exercised against the real auth service under the black-box `prod-in-memory` profile.
2. Same path as an authenticated member -> 200, body shape `GraphDiagnosticReadResponse`: `groupRef.groupId === "__global__"`, `groupRef.applicationId`/`workspaceId` echo the path scope, and `cache: { hit, refreshed }` booleans present. That ordering is an existence-disclosure fact only a black-box recipe can pin.

The diagnostic is computed from process-local caches (`groupStateSnapshotsRepository`, `clientStateSnapshotsRepository`), so this pins whether a non-owning node answers 200 with the same node set or degrades — behaviour no stubbed unit test can observe.

title: Principal `activate` racing the activation criterion's own fenced `activate`
scenario: Create a `managed`-style group with `activation.mode: 'threshold-or-deadline'` and a short `deadlineMs` (~2000 ms), plan, publish, connect. title: Fenced `connect` racing the replan its own membership/presence churn causes — the two 409 connect-conflict codes have zero black-box coverage
scenario: Take api-v1-debounced-replanning.json's already-built fenced connect (it reads GET `/topology` and POSTs `/lifecycle/connect` with `expectedFormationEpoch` + `expectedLayout` = `{groupRevision, presenceRevision, version, state}`). title: Principal `connect` racing the automatic connect trigger — the winner decides whether the durable latch is consumed or stranded
scenario: Create a phased group with `establishment.connectTrigger: {kind: 'after', settleMs: 2000}` (as api-v1-automatic-formation-triggers.json does) so a latch arms at `plan` time and the connect timer petitions at the settle. Then race, in one parallel block: a manager POST `/lifecycle/connect` (fenced on the published layout) against the automation's own connect at the settle instant. Assert both possible orders. If automation wins, the latch moves to `consumed` and the principal's connect returns 403 `lifecycle-transition-invalid` (or 409 stale-epoch when it carries `expectedFormationEpoch`). If the principal wins, `computeGroupConnectTrigger` does NOT consume the latch — only `facts.internalAuthority === 'formation-automation'` reaches the consume arm — and the automation's later petition returns early because `holdsPlannedCandidateAt('connecting')` is false, leaving an `awaiting-publication` row pinned to an epoch the group has already left. Assert the group still reaches `active` and no duplicate connect is dialed.
why_it_matters: Trigger satisfaction is *durably latched* (product decision 32), so a stranded latch is persistent state, not a transient. `petitionAwaitingGroupConnectTriggers` lists only latches at `group.formationEpoch`, so the orphan is never revisited — benign today, but nothing pins that. More importantly, this is the canonical 'application command races a server automatic trigger' case, and the corpus's two automation recipes both deliberately stand back and poll until automation finishes before issuing any command.
evidence_of_absence: api-v1-automatic-formation-triggers.json has 0 parallel steps and its steps are: plan-trigger poll → connect-trigger poll → activate → reconfigure → poll. api-v1-presence-formation-trigger.json likewise has 0 parallel steps. The Python scan of all parallel blocks and fragments found no `/lifecycle/` path anywhere. Server: the consume arm is the first branch of `computeGroupConnectTrigger` in /Users/knuthelge/ProjectLocker/github/ar-eye-hunter/packages/shared-server/rallar-system/group-state/mutation/aggregate/compute-group-connect-trigger.ts; the automation-side early return is `!holdsPlannedCandidateAt(group.lifecycleState)` in `petitionGroupConnectTrigger` at /Users/knuthelge/ProjectLocker/github/ar-eye-hunter/packages/shared-server/rallar-system/topology/replay/work/create-group-connect-trigger-work-handler.ts; `HOLDS_PLANNED_CANDIDATE.connecting === false` in /Users/knuthelge/ProjectLocker/github/ar-eye-hunter/packages/shared/api/group-lifecycle/resolve-formation-stage-entry.ts.

Create a `managed` group overriding `establishment: { planTrigger: {kind:'manual'}, connectTrigger: {kind:'after', settleMs: 8000} }`, join Bob, register both sessions. `POST /lifecycle/plan` -> 200, `lifecycleState: 'planned'`, `formationEpoch: 1`; capture the epoch with `outputs`. Then poll `GET .../formation` past the settle (maxDurationMs > 8000) and assert it is STILL `{ lifecycleState: 'connecting', formationEpoch: 2 }` — this is the load-bearing assertion: it proves the automation's petition dropped on the epoch clause and dialed nothing a second time, even though its `awaiting-publication` latch was never consumed (a principal connect cannot reach the consume arm, which is gated on `facts.internalAuthority === 'formation-automation'`). - The loser's answer is never 409: computeLifecycleTransition comments "Authority first: the fence's answer names the stored plan..." and calls computeLifecycleAuthorityRejection (which runs canCommandGroupLifecycleTransition, i.e. the transition table) BEFORE computeLifecycleFenceRejection; `connecting: { reset: 'dormant', activate: 'active', 'fail-formation': 'forming' }` has no `connect` cell, so it is 403 `lifecycle-transition-invalid` — the status this corpus already pins in api-v1-group-lifecycle-transitions.json's `startFromActiveIsDenied`: `"expect": {"status": 403, "body": {..., "code": "lifecycle-transition-invalid", "status": 403}}`.

title: Two authorized principals commanding the same group at once — `plan|plan` hits the idempotent cell, `connect|connect` hits a typed rejection
scenario: Two variants in one recipe, each a parallel block of two `/lifecycle/` POSTs from two different active members of the same group, with `expect.statusCode: [200, 403]`. title: Concurrent admission decisions on the same pending principal — grant vs decline resolve asymmetrically (400 vs 200 no-op)
scenario: Under `admission.mode: 'manager-approval'`, park a join so the member sits `pending`. Then race, in one parallel block, POST `/admissions/{principalId}/grant/requests/{a}` against POST `/admissions/{principalId}/decline/requests/{b}` — either from two co-equal managers or from the same manager on two nodes. Assert the two legal outcomes and note they are NOT symmetric: if decline commits first, the grant's retry finds `status: 'left'` and `computeGrantGroupAdmission` throws `GroupMutationRejectedError('No pending admission for group member: …')` → 400; if grant commits first, the decline's retry finds `status: 'active'`, falls into `existing?.status !== 'pending'` → `noOp(...)` → 200 with no state change. Assert the final roster holds exactly one status and `activeMemberCount` moved by 0 or 1, never 2.
why_it_matters: Grant and decline are the only two mutually-destructive decisions on one member row, they are reachable by every manager simultaneously, and the outcome the caller sees for 'you lost' differs by 400 vs 200 depending on which command lost. A client that treats 200 as 'my decision applied' would silently mis-report a declined join as declined when it was in fact granted. Both computes route through `computeGroupMembershipWrite`, whose guard is the *group* row revision, so the serialization is real and testable.

title: Reconnect hydration across a lifecycle stage change
scenario: Alice and Bob join a phased group and open sockets while it is FORMING. Alice's socket is dropped (`ws.close`). While she is offline the manager runs `lifecycle/plan` then `lifecycle/activate` (or `lifecycle/reset` + `lifecycle/start`), so the group crosses two stages and its formation epoch advances twice. Alice mints a fresh ws-ticket, reopens, and the recipe asserts the unicast `overlay.topology` hydration she receives names the post-activate layout (and, in the replan variant, that the accepted slot still carries her even though the planned row moved past her), then a floored `/formation` and `/topology` read-through agrees with what the socket delivered.
why_it_matters: `RtcTopologyReconnectHydration.hydrate` (packages/shared-server/rallar-system/topology/replay/hydration/rtc-topology-reconnect-hydration.ts) deliberately scans two namespaces -- planned and accepted -- precisely because "the accepted namespace names members the traffic layout still carries after a replan moved the planned row past them". Nothing black-box proves that second scan matters, or that a reconnecting client is hydrated to the stage the group actually reached rather than the one it left. A regression here silently strands a returning player on a dead layout.
evidence_of_absence: Mapping every recipe's ordered ws.open / ws.close / `/lifecycle/<cmd>/` sequence (python walk over all 52 api-v1 recipes) yields exactly one close-then-reopen recipe, `api-v1-group-state-reconnect-resync.json` -- and `grep -c '/lifecycle/' api-v1-group-state-reconnect-resync.json` returns 0; its offline mutation is `updateGroupWhileAlphaOffline` (a group metadata PUT). The only recipe that closes a socket before lifecycle commands, `api-v1-group-lifecycle-transitions.json`, has sequence `OPEN plan plan CLOSE activate pause reconfigure reconfigure activate plan reset start` -- no OPEN after the CLOSE.
corrected:
Reconnect hydration delivers the post-activate accepted layout, and the corpus asserts no overlay.topology payload at all.

Base recipe (the smallest honest delta on `api-v1-group-lifecycle-transitions.json`): Alice (manager) and Bob join a phased/managed group and both open sockets while it is FORMING; consume the FORMING hydration on Alice (the existing `formingTopologyHydrationArrives`). Close Alice's socket. While she is offline the manager POSTs `lifecycle/plan` then `lifecycle/activate`, so the group runs forming -> planned -> connecting -> active and `formationEpoch` goes 0 -> 3 (assert `lifecycleState: "connecting", formationEpoch: 2` on the floored `/formation` read after plan, and `lifecycleState: "active", formationEpoch: 3` on the activate response — the epoch advances three times, not twice, because the HTTP activate carries the group through the intermediate `connect` cell). Poll `/topology` until `acceptedSnapshot.state == "active"`, capturing `acceptedSnapshot.version` and its `activeSessionIds`. Alice then mints a second ws-ticket for the same session id, reopens, and the recipe asserts the unicast `overlay.topology` frame she receives carries the promoted accepted row — not merely that a frame arrived: `targets.mode == "unicast"`, `targets.toPeerId == {aliceSessionId}`, and the payload's snapshot `version` equal to the captured `acceptedSnapshot.version` with `activeSessionIds` containing `{aliceSessionId}`. Finally a floored `GET /formation` (`lifecycleState: "active"`, `formationEpoch: 3`) and `GET /topology` (`acceptedSnapshot.version` equal to the version the socket delivered) agree with what the socket delivered. The payload assertions are the load-bearing part: a scripted sweep of every ws.wait in the corpus shows not one asserts any overlay.topology payload field beyond `typeId`, so today a hydration that delivered a stale FORMING row, or the wrong group's row, would pass every existing recipe.

title: Logout while a socket is open never exercises the durable forced-disconnect outbox

title: A formation timer or activation clock firing after the group moved on
scenario: Create a phased group with `activation.mode: "deadline"` and a ~6s `deadlineMs`, plan it so the establishment `deadline` timer is armed, then within 2s issue `lifecycle/reset` (or `pause`), which advances `formationEpoch`. Sleep past the original due time and assert the group is still exactly where `reset` put it -- same lifecycleState, same formationEpoch, no new layout version, no activation-status write -- i.e. the fired entry was a stale drop rather than a late transition. Same shape for the `retry` timer (fail below floor, then `reset` before the backoff elapses) and for the `dwell` activation clock (arm a band, then replan so the coverage basis identity changes before the 3s dwell fires).
why_it_matters: Both durable clocks are epoch/basis-fenced by design: formation-timer-outbox-entry.ts states "Every entry carries the post-write epoch, so a group that moves on before the timer fires turns the entry into a stale drop", and activation-status-clock-outbox-entry.ts keys the dwell on `formationEpoch` plus a `coverageBasisLayoutIdentity` hash. `computeGroupLifecycleTransition` advances the epoch on every accepted transition except an idempotent replan. A broken fence is a late timer applying a decision the group already superseded -- the exact class of bug the fence exists to prevent, and one no unit test can prove end to end.
evidence_of_absence: `grep -ln deadlineMs *.json` returns 7 recipes; for each, `grep -c 'lifecycle/reset'` and `grep -c 'lifecycle/start'` are both 0. The only recipe using reset/start is `api-v1-group-lifecycle-transitions.json`, which contains no `deadlineMs` and drives a `managed` (not `phased`) group, so no stage-trigger or deadline entry is ever armed there. `grep -oi dwell *.json` returns 2 hits, both inside `api-v1-group-status-lifecycle.json`'s prose description.
corrected:
Restated gap (three sibling scenarios, one recipe each or one recipe with three groups):

(a) STALE ESTABLISHMENT DEADLINE. Create a group with an explicit policy: `formation: "phased"`, `activation.mode: "deadline"`, `deadlineMs: 6000`, `maxFormationAttempts: 2`. Plan it, publish a layout, `lifecycle/connect` (this arms the `deadline` entry at now+6000 for epoch N, formation-timer-outbox-entry.ts `computeEstablishmentTimerEntries`). Within ~1s issue `lifecycle/reset` and capture `formationEpoch` (N+1) and `formationAttemptCount` from the response. Then a `set` step with `request.delayMs: 8000`, then GET the group and the formation view and assert: `lifecycleState: "dormant"`, `formationEpoch` still N+1, `formationAttemptCount` unchanged, and `activationStatus` not `failed`. The assertion is load-bearing because `evaluateFormationDeadline` submits `failGroupFormation` unconditionally when no active planned layout exists — which is precisely what a reset leaves — so only the `formationEpoch > work.formationEpoch` fence keeps the group where reset put it.

(b) STALE RETRY BACKOFF. Reuse the below-floor-at-deadline shape that `api-v1-group-formation-criterion.json` already drives (`formationBelowFloorAtDeadlineParksTheSpentSeries`) but with an unspent budget, so the failure lands in `forming` and arms a `retry` entry at now+5000 (DEFAULT_FORMATION_RETRY_BACKOFF_MS). (c) STALE DWELL CLOCK. title: connect naming a planned layout the group has already superseded

title: The evidence-expiry heartbeat: a quiet group's coverage decaying with nobody touching it
scenario: Activate a group on a single reported RTT edge (as `api-v1-group-status-lifecycle` does), then stop all traffic and idle for ~70s. Poll `/formation` and the group row and assert the stored `activationStatus` walked down on its own -- the self-rescheduling `evidence-expiry` clock re-reading at +30s, the sample ageing out of the 60s freshness window, and the resulting band being written to the group row by the clock, not by any request. The paired arm re-reports the edge and asserts the `dwell`-gated recovery (`degraded` -> `active` once `dwellSatisfied`) after a further 3s clock cycle.
why_it_matters: `armEvidenceExpiry` (topology/replay/work/group-activation-status-observer.ts) exists because "coverage falls when measurements age out of the freshness window, and that is the absence of evidence, so nothing else would ever wake the group" -- GROUP_ACTIVATION_EVIDENCE_EXPIRY_MS = 30_000, DEFAULT_FORMATION_EVIDENCE_FRESHNESS_MS = 60_000, GROUP_ACTIVATION_STATUS_DWELL_MS = 3_000. title: Late-join non-republication is asserted over HTTP while the founder's socket is open and unwatched
scenario: api-v1-group-topology-late-joiner already holds the founder's socket open across `joinLate`. Add an `absent` ws.wait on that socket for a second `overlay.topology` frame (after consuming the first), and give the late joiner a socket of his own to assert he receives no overlay frame either — since he joined without presence and is not in `activeSessionIds`.
why_it_matters: The recipe's entire claim is in its step name, `readTopologyAsLateJoinerWithoutNewPublication`, yet that claim is checked by comparing two HTTP `GET .../topology` reads. A server that republished an identical snapshot to every peer on every join — the exact flap the formation-epoch design exists to prevent — would pass this recipe unchanged. The corpus has six `absent` ws.wait steps and not one is on `overlay.topology`.
evidence_of_absence: Step-listing api-v1-group-topology-late-joiner.json shows `ws.open openFounderWs` → `ws.wait waitFormationOverlayPublication` → `http joinLate` → `http readTopologyAsLateJoinerWithoutNewPublication` → `ws.close closeFounderWs`; the late joiner registers and logs in but never opens a socket. Enumerating every `absent` ws.wait in the corpus yields exactly six: two `targets.groupRef` scope checks (api-v1-cross-application-ws-isolation), two `targets.principalRef` checks (api-v1-cross-principal-client-state-isolation), and two `id.msgId` checks (api-v1-group-data-policy). None mentions `overlay.topology`.
corrected:
Extend api-v1-group-topology-late-joiner.json so non-republication is asserted on the wire, not only inferred from an HTTP version equality:

1. Add `"consume": true` to the existing `waitFormationOverlayPublication` step, so the formation frame is removed from the wsFounder buffer (waitForWsMessageAbsence rescans the whole buffer and would otherwise re-match it).
2. Declare a second ws connection `wsLate`, mint a ws-ticket for the late joiner's session, and open his socket BEFORE `joinLate` — he registers and logs in today but never connects.
3. After `joinLate` and `readTopologyAsLateJoinerWithoutNewPublication`, add two `absent` ws.wait steps with a `withinMs` window comfortably longer than the topology recompute debounce (4000 ms, matching api-v1-cross-application-ws-isolation's window):
   - on `wsFounder`: absent `{ "route": { "topicId": "overlay.topology" }, "payload": { "typeId": "overlay.topology" } }` — pinning that a membership delta which leaves activeSessionIds unchanged takes the `skipped-unchanged` branch and republishes nothing to the already-formed member (M8).
   - on `wsLate`: the same absent matcher — pinning that a member who joined without a presence transition is in neither the reconnect-hydration candidate set nor the room broadcast audience, because both filter on `activeSessionIds` / live `activeSessions`.
4. Close `wsLate` alongside `closeFounderWs`, and update the recipe-matrix description, which currently advertises the omission ("no new publication awaited").

What this adds over the current recipe: the HTTP read only proves no new topology *version* was minted; it cannot distinguish "no publication" from "a republication carrying the same version but an advanced source causal revision", and it races the asynchronous replan because it fires immediately after joinLate. The two absent waits close both holes, and the late-joiner socket is the only place in the corpus where a group member holding an open socket without presence is observed at all.
